operative_text.controlling:
10.49(1)  The Court may order a party, lawyer or other person to
pay to the court clerk a penalty in an amount determined by the
Court if
(a) the party, lawyer or other person contravenes or fails to
comply with these rules or a practice note or direction of
the Court without adequate excuse, and
(b) the contravention or failure to comply, in the Court’s
opinion, has interfered with or may interfere with the
proper or efficient administration of justice.
(2)  The order applies despite
(a) a settlement of the action, or
(b) an agreement to the contrary by the parties.

BOOK_A.commentary:
This Rule is designed to provide a penalty for misconduct where the opposing party is
complicit, or is not harmed.¹
Mere failure to follow Rules etc. is not enough; interference with
the administration of justice is needed.²
Are procedural safeguards akin to those for contempt,
needed?³
An example would be an agreement to call a long trial a short one, to get an early trial date,
with resulting harm to other litigants when the trial runs over time. An adjournment of a special
chambers hearing because of late ﬁling of an afﬁdavit led to costs jointly against the counsel and
his client.⁴
Rule 3.3 requires commencement in the judicial centre speciﬁed, without waiting for the
defendant to complain. The court can transfer the suit to the right judicial centre on its own motion,
with costs under R.10.49.⁵
This Rule was used to make each counsel pay $250.00 to the Registrar for failure to transcribe
recorded reasons of the judge appealed from, in two appeals.⁶
Costs were assessed for not
speaking to the appeal list in a case involving children.⁷
And for causing a judicial dispute resolution
session to be cancelled at the last minute.⁸
And for not disclosing when getting an order nisi of
foreclosure, commencement in the wrong judicial district.⁹
This Rule was used for repeatedly
disobeying court orders and ﬁling forbidden documents,¹⁰
and for three times letting a criminal
appeal be dismissed and getting three restorations.¹¹
There is a review of the previous cases using
this Rule.¹²
This Rule does not apply to one side’s failure to pay costs previously awarded to the other
party.¹³
This Rule cannot be used to order a payment to another party.¹⁴
This Rule might allow a daily penalty.¹⁵
Misconduct by a solicitor led to a $1, 000 penalty under
R.10.49, plus costs of 4 times column 1 of Schedule C to the opposing party.¹⁶

Rule 10.49 was used (plus costs to the innocent party) in light of R.1.2, where court directions
were disobeyed but contempt could not be found for evidentiary and technical reasons.¹
One issue raised had already been decided against this would-be appellant in this litigation,
which was a collateral attack. This self-represented litigant was previously warned about
relitigating the same issues and was doing it again. A penalty of $2500 was ordered paid to the
Clerk of the Court under R.10.49(1). If this litigant persisted in that, the penalties would probably
grow.²
A litigant kept expressly rejecting advice from court ofﬁcials about how and where to appeal
a decision of a chambers judge, and used insults and threats and did not comply with even the
simplest requirements. Court resources are not inﬁnite. So $2000 penalty for contravening rules
under R.10.49(1) was levied.³
Lawyers “notarizing” odd pseudolegal documents for self-represented litigants have had to
pay costs under this Rule.⁴
If the offending party is the government, ordering costs to the Clerk or Registrar is pointless,
and the court may order costs to the opposing party instead.⁵
“Costs” or “security for costs” usually refer to moneys payable by one party to another (for
litigation expenses, not to a sum imposed under R.10.49 and payable to the Clerk of the Court),
and so payment of R.10.49 awards has no priority in payment out of an existing fund held as
security for costs.⁶

BOOK_B.title: Penalty for contravening rules

commentary.text: Rule 10.49 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.49. 1. Overview In H2 Canmore Apartments LP v. Cormode & Dickson Construction Edmonton Ltd., 2024 ABKB 424, Justice Marion gave this overview of the Rule: [124] The public policy behind these rules is to ensure that court orders are obeyed which, in turn, upholds the policy of promoting the public interest in the fair and just resolution of claims in a timely and cost-effective way: rule 1.2; Osborn at para 35; 336239 Alberta Ltd (Dave’s Diesel Repair) v Mella, 2016 ABQB 174 at para 35. [125] Rule 10.49 differs from rule 5.12 because, if a penalty is levied, it is paid to the Clerk of the Court, not the other parties: rule 10.49(1); Makis v Alberta Health Services, 2020 ABCA 168 at para 66; Carnwell v Carnwell, 2024 ABKB 318 at para 26. It is also different than a penalty or sanction for contempt under rule 10.52 and, when read together with the fundamental rules, provides the Court with a helpful and “very flexible tool”, and likely a more efficient and effective sanctioning process: rules 1.2-1.5; CJD v RIJ, 2018 ABQB 287 at paras 62-66; rules 1.2-1.5; Meads v Meads, 2012 ABQB 571 at paras 604-607. [126] Rule 10.49 requires three things: (1) contravention or failure to comply with the Rules, a practice note or a court direction; (2) without adequate excuse; and (3) the contravention or failure has, in the Court’s opinion, interfered with or may interfere with the proper or efficient administration of justice. It does not require that the contravention or failure be intentional: Baxter v Darby, 2009 ABQB 559 (Master) at para 12. [127] The meaning of “without adequate excuse” has not been expressly considered by this Court. Although the wording is slightly different, I find that a similarly high bar set for “sufficient cause” under rule 5.12 is also reasonable for “without adequate excuse” under rule 10.49. Parties must establish, at a minimum, that, even with reasonable due diligence, they could not comply with the Rules, practice note or court direction due to something outside their control. Interpreting “adequate excuse” this way will not cause injustice or unfairness because the Court retains the discretion to not impose a penalty even in the absence of an adequate excuse: Morin v TransAlta Utilities Corporation, 2017 ABQB 409 at para 49. [128] With respect to the meaning of “interfered with or may interfere with the proper administration of justice”, this is the same wording as under former rule 599.1. There must be evidence to support a finding of past or future interference: Estate of Montgomery, 2019 ABQB 833 at para 45. [129] Interfering with the proper or efficient administration of justice can include interfering with the judicial function, court operations, or actions administered by the Court, in particular in the form of wasted public resources or delay in the progress of court proceedings: Milfive Investments v Sefel, 1998 ABCA 164 at para 3; Pollock v Liberty Technical Services Ltd, 1997 CanLII 14782 (AB KB) at para 14; Morin at paras 50-51; Trang v Alberta (Edmonton Remand Centre), 2007 ABCA 267 at para 14, leave to appeal to SCC refused, 2008 CanLII 6439; Klushin v Tkachuk, 2001 ABCA 231 at paras 14-17; CJD at para 70. [130] Specifically, interfering with the proper or efficient administration of justice can include a failure to honour records discovery obligations: Weatherford Canada Partnership v Addie, 2010 ABQB 477 [Weatherford QB] at para 53 aff’d 2010 ABCA 362 [Weatherford CA]; Goofers (Theroux) v Goofers, 2002 ABQB 1094 at para 56. [131] Non-exhaustive factors relevant to whether to impose a penalty under rule 10.49 (and the quantum of any penalty) include: (a) any delay, inefficiencies or increased expenses caused by the contravention/failure: Weatherford QB at para 53; Pollock at para 14; Meads at para 604; (b) the impact of the contravention/failure on the judicial function and court operations, including the waste of public resources: Milfive at para 3; Klushin at para 14; Trang at para 14; Pollock at para 14; AS v NLH, 2006 ABQB 708 at paras 17-19; CJD at para 70; (c) the reasonableness of the explanation for the contravention/failure, including whether the party reasonably attempted to avoid contravention, or to comply, or whether the contravention/failure was vexatious, intentional, careless or innocent: Weatherford CA at para 10; R v Ayyazi, 2022 ABKB 836 at paras 60-63; Royal Bank of Canada v Anderson, 2023 ABKB 661 at paras 21-23, 42; Morin at para 50-51; Baxter at para 12; Meads at para 607; (d) the need to impose a penalty to secure compliance: Demb v Valhalla Group Ltd, 2015 ABCA 29 [Demb 2015 CA] at para 40 (O’Ferrall, JA concurring in result); Ubah v Ubah, 2024 ABKB 164 at para 35; (e) the need for general or specific deterrence, including whether the contravention/failure represents an undesirable general litigation practice or a pattern of conduct of a specific party or counsel: Demb 2015 CA at para 40 (O’Ferrall, JA concurring in result); Milfive at para 3; Hunter v Preston, 2001 ABCA 35 at para 21; McClelland v Harrison, 2023 ABKB 638 at para 14; Morin at paras 50-51; Crouser-Reymon v Tawa Developments Inc, 2010 ABQB 166 at paras 23-26; (f) the need to punish, discipline or denounce: Lastiwka v TD Waterhouse Investor Services (Canada) Inc, 2006 ABQB 567 at para 78; Wagner at para 19; and (g) the financial means of the party being sanctioned. A penalty under rule 10.49 is not usually intended to impact the substance of the action or create a barrier to non-vexatious access to justice: Osborn at para 46; Meads at para 605. [132] I agree with the sentiments of Stinson J in Apotex Inc v Eli Lilly and Company, 2014 ONSC 3574 at para 4: [4] As stewards of the justice system, both judges and lawyers have a duty to ensure that disputes are resolved and claims are prosecuted in an efficient fashion, so that the limited resources of the court may be effectively shared among all who seek access to justice. [:.] [133] One way we can fulfil our stewardship role, while also protecting against waste of precious private and public resources, is to order rule 10.49 penalties, where appropriate, to promote rule-compliance and to deter and denounce wasteful conduct that causes delay, increases private and public costs, and reduces access to justice. In Baltimore v. Baltimore (1997), 47 Alta. L.R. (3d) 254 (Master), Master Laycock had before him a dispute over the location of a proposed cross examination on affidavit. Counsel could not agree on the location. On the advice of counsel, the respondent did not attend a cross-examination in spite of being served with an appointment and conduct money. Master Laycock held that the respondent's counsel should have brought an application to set aside the appointment if she believed it to be improper. He further held that she was wrong to simply advise her client not to attend the examination. In the course of his reasons for ruling, the learned Master commented, at p. 258, on then R. 599.1: Mr. Baltimore filed an affidavit attempting to explain his non-attendance at the examination on January 10, 1997 and his refusal to attend the cross-examination in Whitecourt. His failure to attend appears to be more a power struggle between counsel and therefore the costs of the application were maintained at a moderate level. It is this power struggle between counsel which brings the profession into disrepute. The application by Mr. McConnel [applicant's counsel] should not have been necessary. Mr. Baltimore on instruction from counsel has failed to comply with the Rules of Court. Pursuant to Rule 599.1(1)(b), this failure to comply “has interfered with or may interfere with the proper or efficient administration of justice.” In these circumstances the court could on its own motion direct counsel to pay to the Clerk of the Court a penalty in the form of costs. I make these comments with respect to Rule 599.1 to bring its existence to the attention of counsel and in this situation the court could well determine that substantial costs [are] payable to the Clerk of the Court. In Pollock v. Liberty Technical Services Ltd. (1997), 50 Alta. L.R. (3d) 335 (Master), Master Laycock invoked the rule when counsel failed to comply with a practice note issued by the Calgary Masters. Master Laycock ordered that the plaintiff and plaintiff's counsel be jointly liable to pay to the Clerk of the Court the sum of $400 as a penalty under the rule. The Court of Appeal has also resorted to the rule. In Milfive Investments Ltd. v. Sefel (1998), 62 Alta. L.R. (3d) 369 (C.A.); [additional reasons to (1998) 216 A.R. 196 (C.A.)], the court heard an appeal from a chambers decision. Counsel had failed to order a transcript of the learned chambers judge's reasons. The court ordered each side to pay the Deputy Registrar the sum of $150 and directed that neither side would be entitled to collect it as a taxable cost. The court said, at p. 370: The Chambers Judge gave extended oral reasons, which were tape-recorded, as is usual. Neither party thought to ask to have them transcribed, and the agreement as to contents signed by both parties omits them. We had three such cases this week in Calgary, necessitating last-minute transcription. That caused this Court and the judges appealed from a good deal of inconvenience. We have mentioned this problem before in at least one reported decision. It is time to reinforce our sermons with penance. We rely on R. 599.1, but at this early stage we keep the amounts low. Each side will pay to the Deputy Registrar in Calgary the sum of $150.00, and this will not be taxable as a disbursement in computing party-party costs in future. In Hunter v. Preston (2001), 277 A.R. 151 (C.A.), Côté J.A. invoked the rule in a case of failure to speak to the appeal list, and ordered the appellant's and respondent's counsel to each pay costs ($350 and $100 respectively). In Trang v. Alberta (Director, Edmonton Remand Centre), 2007 ABCA 267, 2007 CarswellAlta 1098, 412 A.R. 276, 79 Alta. L.R. (4th) 21, counsel for the respondents was ordered to personally pay costs of $1000 under then Rule 599.1. Counsel had arranged for an expedited appeal hearing, but then took on a conflicting obligation for a new client, Mr. K., without arranging for other counsel to attend and conduct the expedited appeal hearing. The appeal had to be adjourned. The Court of Appeal, in awarding costs personally against counsel, said, at p. 27, “Without firm workable arrangements for substitute counsel on this appeal, [Counsel] should not have accepted Mr. K.'s new overseas work, abandoning the Court and over 20 existing clients in Edmonton.” Using R. 10.49 as an Alternative to Contempt Proceedings In CJD v. RIJ, 2018 ABQB 287, 2018 CarswellAlta 715, Justice Graesser had before him an application to find RIJ in contempt “for failing to comply with an order” made by the learned case management judge on January 9, 2018. Justice Graesser concluded that he could not find RIJ in contempt of the order because RIJ did not have actual knowledge of it. However, his Lordship relied on Rule 10.49 to impose a penalty of $1,000 for RIJ's failure to comply with a direction (dated December 5, 2017) of which he did have knowledge. Justice Graesser discussed the utility of using Rule 10.49 as opposed to the contempt rules: 63 In the context of Rule 1.2(2)(e), that the Rules “provide an effective, efficient and credible system of remedies and sanctions to enforce these rules and orders and judgments,” contempt remedies are frequently neither effective nor efficient. A declaration of contempt is often a paper tiger. Being jailed for civil contempt is now the last resort consequence for a last resort remedy, following Carey. 64 The process to obtain a contempt order is costly and timely and requires proof on the criminal standard. There is nothing efficient about that. It requires personal service, which is difficult when the respondent is evading service, as is the case here. As a result, I think a lot of time, energy and money are frequently being spent on a remedy that is rarely granted, and even when granted is rarely effective. Justice Graesser set out the provisions of R. 10.49, and said: 66 In my view, this rule must be read in conjunction with the foundational rules. This remedy was added when the new Rules of Court were proclaimed in 2010. In addition to a rigorous approach to costs when a litigant (represented or self-represented) is playing games with the court process, there are alternate approaches to contempt that may be equally if not more efficient and effective. 67 Here, RIJ failed to comply with my clear direction of December 5, 2017. He had actual notice of that direction as he specifically responded to it on December 10. RIJ then dodged service of process by unilaterally choosing to disregard an email account he had provided for court purposes and which was the court-ordered means of service on him. 68 In these circumstances, it is appropriate to order RIJ to pay a penalty to the Court in the amount of $1,000. I use a somewhat modest amount having regard to his apparent financial means. … … 70 Having regard to the waste of the Court's time and resources dealing with RIJ's intransigence in providing CJD with information she is entitled to, it is necessary to send him and others a message that court process cannot be abused. 71 Non payment of this amount to the Clerk of the Court may be a factor in whether or not RIJ is permitted to make any further applications in this matter. 72 I also award CJD $1,500 in costs. I choose a global amount that reflects the enormous waste of time and energy she has been put to as a result of RIJ's game-playing, failure to comply with my direction and the rules regarding service. 2. Missed deadline in criminal appeal In R. v. Simpson, 2024 ABCA 53, a criminal appeal, a penalty was imposed for the failure to meet filing deadlines. Justice Slatter noted that this “may be the first time in which a penalty has been imposed for the failure to meet filing deadlines in a criminal appeal.” His Lordship said that since this was the first such imposition, “a modest penalty was imposed in this case, although this does not necessarily set the standard for future cases.” (paragraph 10) 3. Court must give notice to affected person if matter raised on Court’s own motion In Kotyk (Re), 2024 ABCA 233, a trial court judge had, on his own motion and without notice to the affected person, made an order under Rule 10.49 directing a lawyer to pay a $5000 penalty for notarizing a “pseudolaw” document. The Court of Appeal reiterated that the rules of natural justice bind courts as well as administrative tribunals. The Court said: [16] The audi alteram partem rule is a rule of natural justice and one of the fundamental tenets of our legal system. It requires parties be given adequate notice of the case against them and a fair opportunity to be heard before judgment is rendered. Parties are afforded the opportunity to correct or contradict factual statements prejudicial to their positions, and to answer contrary arguments on matters of law: A(LL) v B (A), 1995 CanLII 52 (SCC), [1995] 4 SCR 536 at para 27 [A(LL)]; Malton at paras 28, 35, 37; JM v EM, 2022 ABCA 49 at para 48; and R v Nahanee, 2022 SCC 37 at paras 54, 55. [17] Although the rules of natural justice and procedural fairness are most often discussed in the context of administrative tribunals, courts are no less bound to comply with them: A(LL) at para 27; Malton at para 35. [18] As a general rule, when a court raises a matter on its own motion it must give the affected parties adequate warning of its intention and afford them a fair opportunity to present evidence and argue their position: Whelan v Whelan, 2007 ABCA 282 at paras 5–6; Canada Trustco Mortgage Co v Renard, 2008 BCCA 343 at paras 38–39; Kirk v Kirk, 2017 SKCA 97 at para 29; Province of New Brunswick, as represented by the Minister of Justice v JF, 2021 NBCA 61 at para 34; Yashcheshen v Canada (Attorney General), 2021 SKCA 116 at para 81; Hutton v Hutton, 2021 BCCA 170 at para 14. [19] Finding improper conduct on the part of counsel is a serious matter. Counsel should be given an opportunity to respond: Balogun v Pandher, 2021 ABCA 422 at para 76; Malton at paras 40, 65. For example, the Supreme Court of Canada in Quebec (Director of Criminal and Penal Prosecutions) v Jodoin, 2017 SCC 26 at paras 35–36 emphasized the importance of providing notice and an opportunity to respond where costs are awarded against lawyers: [A] lawyer upon whom such a sanction may be imposed should be given prior notice of the allegations against him or her and the possible consequences. The notice should contain sufficient information about the alleged facts and the nature of the evidence in support of those facts. The notice should be sent far enough in advance to enable the lawyer to prepare adequately. The lawyer should, of course, have an opportunity to make separate submissions on costs and to adduce any relevant evidence in this regard. [Emphasis added]

commentary.text:
Rule 10.49 requires not only a breach, but also proof that the breach will interfere with the administration of justice. Osborn v. Gagne, [2017] A.J. No. 721, 2017 ABQB 438 at para. 3 (Alta. Q.B.), followed in Montgomery Estate v. Montgomery, [2019] A.J. No. 1495, 2019 ABQB 833 at paras. 44-45 (Alta. Q.B.). The rule requires three things: (1) contravention or failure to comply with the Rules, a practice note or a court direction; (2) without adequate excuse; and (3) the contravention or failure has, in the court’s opinion, interfered with or may interfere with the proper or efficient administration of justice. It does not require that the contravention or failure be intentional. H2 Canmore Apartments LP v. Cormode & Dickson Construction Edmonton Ltd., [2024] A.J. No. 898, 2024 ABKB 424 at para. 126 (Alta. K.B.).
Rule 10.49 is designed to monetarily sanction misbehaviour. Osborn v. Gagne, [2017] A.J. No. 721, 2017 ABQB 438 at para. 27 (Alta. Q.B.). Another objective of this rule is to deter further abuse. Bonville v. President’s Choice Financial, [2024] A.J. No. 1004, 2024 ABKB 483 at para. 112 (Alta. K.B.). Rule 10.49 replaced rule 599.1. The penalty or costs award is to be paid to the clerk of the court rather than to the litigant.
